# cli.sgit.ai

> The documentation for sgit, the command-line tool for encrypted vaults (pip install sgit-ai; entry
> points `sgit` and `sgit-ai`): every command, generated from the CLI's own parser; the HTTP API it is a
> client of; the guides; and the CLI team's research, published as articles.

Site version: v0.2.15 · command reference generated from sgit-ai v0.25.0 (165 commands) · 154 pages.

Every page below is markdown, generated from the same source as the HTML page at the same path (swap
`.md` for `.html`). Links inside the markdown point at markdown. Every page in one document: /llms-full.txt.

Notes for agents:
- The command reference is the code's own account of itself: /reference/sgit-cli-reference.json is the
  output of `sgit help all --format json` (schema sgit-cli-reference-v1). Diff two releases' JSON to see
  exactly what changed. Your installed version answers the same question: `sgit help all --format json`.
- Never write a vault key into a tracked file. Read keys may be published; vault keys never.
- The project, the vault platform and the network of sites: https://sgit.ai/llms.txt

## Home
- [cli.sgit.ai](/index.md): The documentation for sgit, the command-line tool for encrypted vaults: every command generated from the CLI's own parser, the HTTP API it is a client of, the guides, and the CLI team's research as articles.

## Get started
- [Docs](/docs/index.md): Every page of the sgit CLI documentation in reading order: getting started, the guides, and the security pages, with the command reference and the HTTP API alongside.
- [What is sgit](/docs/what-is-sgit.md): sgit is git for encrypted vaults: how it works, what makes it different from git, and the ecosystem around it.
- [Installation](/docs/installation.md): Install sgit with pip, verify with sgit doctor, upgrade with sgit update. Python 3.11+, two runtime dependencies.
- [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart.md): From zero to a synced, encrypted, versioned vault in five minutes: create, commit, push, clone, pull.
- [sgit for git users](/docs/sgit-for-git-users.md): The Rosetta stone: every git command mapped to its sgit equivalent, plus the three deliberate differences.
- [The two-branch model](/docs/two-branch-model.md): sgit's central idea: private clone branches per machine or agent, shared named branches, and explicit publishing.
- [When NOT to use sgit](/docs/limitations.md): The honest page: sgit's edges, stated plainly, plus the current roadmap gaps.

## Guides
- [Partial clones: a folder scope and a history depth](/docs/partial-clones.md): sgit clone --path holds one folder and carries the rest by id; --depth holds the newest commits only. Measured on a 600-commit vault: one folder in 14 s against 80 s for the whole vault. The rules, widening with sgit fetch, the commands that need a full clone, and the two edges.
- [Pack mode: a playbook for agents](/docs/pack-mode-for-agents.md): Everything an agent needs to use sgit pack vaults (sgit-ai 0.24.0 and later) in a project, as recipes to follow in order. Decide whether a vault should be a pack vault; create one, or convert a copy of an existing vault and cut a team over to it; the daily loop and what its output should look like; who compacts, when, and how; the patterns for CI jobs, many agents, read-only readers and throwaway vaults; the health checks; every error message an agent will meet, with what to do; what never to do; and a block to paste into an agent's own instructions.
- [History integrity: the format gate, verifying signatures, and rewinds](/docs/history-integrity.md): sgit vault format (format 2, 128-bit ids, --min-client), who can open a raised vault and what old clients say, the shared branch index, rewind detection and --accept-rewind, sgit check verify, signatures-required and what a signature proves, and a checklist for raising a vault. For sgit-ai 0.21.0.
- [Working with AI agents](/docs/agents.md): The agent-facing surface: sgit write, --json everywhere, the clone modes including scoped and shallow clones, the session pattern, and multi-agent collaboration.
- [Agents sharing one vault](/docs/agents-sharing-one-vault.md): The loop for a team of agents on one vault with sgit-ai 0.18.0: a scoped shallow clone per session, status before commit, push that pulls first, and the full table of what a pull does with uncommitted work: kept when untouched, refused by name when it would be overwritten.
- [Sending messages between vaults](/docs/vault-messaging.md): How two vaults exchange encrypted messages without sharing a vault key and without the sender holding an account: append lanes addressed by a token, composed with PKI. Worked example in CLI, curl and sg.append, with the one step that is not yet wired marked PROPOSED.
- [Append-lane messaging between agents that hold no one else's vault key](/docs/append-lane-messaging.md): The write-up of two-way, signed and encrypted messaging between agents over sgit's append lanes, as two teams ran it on 25 and 26 September 2026: per-session signing keys with a pinned key registry on the sender's own site, ephemeral inbox vaults for agents that keep no secret, the flows, security properties, threat model, HTTP calls as observed, eleven places sgit.ai's docs differed, and recommendations for sgit. Relayed by sgit.newsroom.sgit.ai.
- [Self-hosting a vault server for agents](/docs/self-host-for-agents.md): Encrypted memory for agents in VMs, containers, a Mac mini or ephemeral jobs: run the SG/Send container with an access token and a storage folder, create the vault, the agent's clone-work-push entry point, Docker Compose, Kubernetes manifests, the cloud, a second server, what the server holds, and the errors you may meet (--endpoint, mcp<2, port 8080).
- [Send a vault key to the registry](/docs/send-a-vault-key.md): For an agent that holds SG/Send vault keys and was given this page, an inbox vault id and an append token: the rules (never display a key, never improvise a route), the vault-key-handover/v1 payload, the registry's public key and endpoint, a sender script that pins the key's fingerprint, what to do afterwards and on a 404. The id and the token are never published.
- [sgit-ai 0.25.0 release notes: large vaults](/docs/update-to-0-25-0.md): Release notes for sgit-ai 0.25.0, for people and agents. On a large vault, the cost of a command now follows the change, not the vault. On a vault of 76,000 files a one-file commit went from 29 minutes to under 5 seconds and a status from 71 seconds to about 4. What changed (trees read as JSON, the flattened head cached, a linear and incremental tree builder, a scan cache keyed like git's index, no tree walk when a push's server has nothing new, history log by tree diff), the data-loss bug a review found in the first version of the scan cache and how it was closed, the two new cache files and what they hold, and what is still slow. Nothing changes on the server or in a vault's format.
- [Using sgit from Claude on a Team or Enterprise plan: the network allowlist](/docs/how-to/claude-team-egress.md): On Claude Team and Enterprise plans an Owner sets the code sandbox's network access for the whole organisation, and the default blocks every sgit host. Which domains to allow (apex domains explicitly), how to check from inside a session, how a proxy's CONNECT 403 differs from a server outage, and why web fetch can read sgit.ai while the shell cannot.
- [sgit-ai 0.24.0 release notes: pack mode](/docs/update-to-0-24-0.md): Release notes for sgit-ai 0.24.0, for people and agents. Pack mode is new and opt-in: a vault whose objects travel as zips, cloned in a handful of requests whatever its history, with files compressed before they are encrypted. The commands (init --packs, pack import, export, compact, ls, stats, verify), what was measured, the gate that refuses older clients by name, what does not work on a pack vault yet, the two transport changes every vault gets, and how the release was reviewed. Normal vaults behave as before.
- [Update sgit-ai to 0.21.0](/docs/update-to-0-21-0.md): For an agent team: sgit update, what now refuses and what to do (symlinks, unreadable files, SGIT_DEFAULT_BASE_URL, key zips, branch names, rewinds, signatures), the new history commands (undo, reflog, amend, revert --as-commit, shorthand, log filters), signed tags, --force-with-lease, notes for vault owners and mixed 0.20/0.21 teams. Covers 0.19.0 and 0.20.0. Published 11 October 2026.
- [Update sgit-ai to 0.18.0](/docs/update-to-0-18-0.md): Five minutes for an agent team: sgit update, check the version, change the clone command to --path and --depth, and what to do when a pull is refused. Published 7 October 2026.

## Security
- [Security model](/security/index.md): sgit's zero-knowledge security model, precisely stated: the crypto stack, what the server can and cannot see, key strength, and the open security process.
- [Vault key management: where each key lives, and how it travels](/docs/key-management.md): The reference for sgit-ai v0.20.0: each kind of credential and where it belongs, how a key travels without entering a chat, giving a key to an agent when platforms have no per-session secrets, rotation with rekey and move, and the local alias store.
- [Vault credentials: what each one can do, and what its prefix declares](/docs/credentials.md): Two capabilities, a vault key that reads and writes and a read key derived from it one way, plus the five prefixes that declare which you are holding and whether it was meant to be published. Why sgit_public_read_ is the form for an open vault, why publishing one under sgit_private_read_ is a mislabel that an agent will correctly refuse, and why the word matters when the bytes are identical.
- [Keys, signatures and encrypting to someone else](/docs/pki.md): The keypair lifecycle run end to end on the shipped CLI: RSA-OAEP 4096 encryption, ECDSA P-256 signing, the JSON public-key bundle, the hybrid envelope format, and what PKI does not do yet.

## Command reference
- [Command reference](/reference/index.md): Every sgit command, subcommand, argument and option, generated from the CLI's own parser (sgit help all --format json), grouped by what it is for.
- [sgit branch](/reference/branch.md): Branch management
- [sgit cache](/reference/cache.md): Declare cached paths (fast single-request reads)
- [sgit cat](/reference/cat.md): Decrypt and print a vault file to stdout
- [sgit check](/reference/check.md): Vault integrity checks
- [sgit clone](/reference/clone.md): Clone a vault from the remote server
- [sgit clone-branch](/reference/clone-branch.md): Thin clone: full commit history + HEAD trees/blobs only. Note: only HEAD is fully fetched — run 'sgit fetch <path>' or 'sgit pull' to access older history.
- [sgit clone-headless](/reference/clone-headless.md): Credentials-only clone: derive keys, write config, no data
- [sgit clone-range](/reference/clone-range.md): Clone a specific commit range (range_from..range_to)
- [sgit commit](/reference/commit.md): Commit local changes to the clone branch
- [sgit create](/reference/create.md): Create a new vault and push it to the server in one step
- [sgit dev](/reference/dev.md): Dev/perf instrumentation tools (sgit dev <tool>)
- [sgit doctor](/reference/doctor.md): Check remote connectivity and configuration
- [sgit fetch](/reference/fetch.md): Fetch file content on demand (sparse clone)
- [sgit file](/reference/file.md): File operations (cat, ls, write)
- [sgit help](/reference/help.md): Show help (use `sgit help all` for full surface)
- [sgit history](/reference/history.md): Commit history and diffs
- [sgit init](/reference/init.md): Create a new empty vault and register it on the server
- [sgit inspect](/reference/inspect.md): Read-only vault inspection tools
- [sgit ls](/reference/ls.md): List vault files with fetch status
- [sgit merge-abort](/reference/merge-abort.md): Abort an in-progress merge and restore working tree
- [sgit migrate](/reference/migrate.md): Run vault data migrations
- [sgit pack](/reference/pack.md): Pack vaults: objects as zips on the host (import, export, compact, ls, verify, stats)
- [sgit pki](/reference/pki.md): PKI key management and encryption
- [sgit publish](/reference/publish.md): Generate the plaintext surface for static publishing (.sg_vault/publish/ — the only path that changes)
- [sgit pull](/reference/pull.md): Pull named branch changes and merge into clone branch
- [sgit push](/reference/push.md): Push clone branch to the named branch
- [sgit remote](/reference/remote.md): Manage vault remotes (alias for `sgit vault remote`)
- [sgit resolve](/reference/resolve.md): Resolve merge conflicts per file or all at once
- [sgit serve](/reference/serve.md): Run this vault on your machine: the vault UI + API in a container (Docker, Podman, Apple container), or --static
- [sgit status](/reference/status.md): Show uncommitted changes in working directory
- [sgit update](/reference/update.md): Update sgit-ai to the latest version
- [sgit vault](/reference/vault.md): Vault management and credential store
- [sgit version](/reference/version.md): Show sgit-ai version
- [sgit write](/reference/write.md): Write a file directly to vault HEAD (agent workflow)

## HTTP API
- [The HTTP API](/api/index.md): The protocol surface behind sgit: base URL, the capability model, and the reference for vault objects, append lanes, authentication headers and error codes. Built from a code-verified audit at v0.33.54, with unresolved endpoints labelled rather than guessed at.
- [Authentication](/api/authentication.md): The six authentication headers, what each one gates, and the hash-comparison model: the server stores SHA-256 of every capability key and never holds a raw key or a private key. Includes why vault reads are open by default.
- [Vault objects](/api/vault-objects.md): The pointer store: read, write, batch, destroy and presigned endpoints, the caching contract that separates immutable content-addressed objects from mutable refs, and the storage layout behind every vault.
- [The transfer API, one encrypted handover, one link](/api/transfers.md): The other API family on this host: a single encrypted payload uploaded once and shared as one link. The two secrets that must not be confused, the SGMETA envelope that keeps the filename off the server, the three calls, revocation that is opt-in at create time only, and when a transfer beats a vault.
- [Append lanes](/api/append-lanes.md): The six append endpoints) the write-only vault-to-vault message transport. Four separated capabilities, the blind write response, server-assigned sortable filenames, idempotent mark-processed, and the limits.
- [Errors and limits](/api/errors.md): 400, 403, 413 and 507: what each means, why a malformed token returns 400 rather than 403, the input patterns enforced before storage is reached, and every documented ceiling.

## Research topics
- [Keys, members and who may write](/research/topics/keys.md): Should the read key and the write key become key pairs, can a vault have members who join and leave by a file each, and can a vault enforce who writes where? What is built, what is designed, and what is still a question.
- [History integrity and signatures](/research/topics/integrity.md): How sgit made a vault's history verifiable without a vault move: signed commits, a format gate, rewind detection, and the compatibility rule that a newer client must never break an older one still writing.
- [Big vaults and many agents](/research/topics/scale.md): What happens when a vault reaches 35,000 objects and ten agents use it every day: what a clone fetches, what each session costs, which fixes came from measuring it, and why the server can stay simple.
- [How a vault takes writes](/research/topics/write-path.md): One commit per change is right for documents and wrong for a stream, and many small objects cost a request each. Copy-on-write, a write-ahead append lane, a vault in one zip, and pack mode, a zip per push, shipped in 0.24.0: what sgit already does, and what is proposed.
- [Running a vault locally](/research/topics/serve.md): How to run a working vault, UI and API, on your own machine: the research into the server's API, the decision to run the SG/Send container rather than re-implement it, and the runtimes sgit supports.
- [Reviewing sgit's security with tools and agents](/research/topics/security-review.md): A tool-assisted security review of the code the zero-knowledge guarantee lives in: which agent skills and threat-modelling tools were worth running, what each found, and a CI pipeline where an AI review can break the build.
- [Found in daily use](/research/topics/correctness.md): The bugs that agents and people hit while using sgit every day, each traced to its cause in the code, with what was fixed and what is still open.

## Research documents
- [Research](/research/index.md): The sgit CLI team's research, kept as written and grouped into topics: measurements on real vaults, designs and the reviews that corrected them, security reviews, and the bugs found in daily use, each with its source in the CLI repository.
- [Graph and index measurements, 26 October 2026: every number, how it was taken, and the scripts to take it again](/research/graph-and-index-measurements-2026-10-26.md): The record of one day's measurements behind three articles: indexes carried in packs, nine graph engines on a vault's triples, and indexes the writer pays for. Every table, including the runs that failed and the numbers the articles left out, with the machine, the versions and a link to the scripts and raw results kept in this site's repository.
- [Architecture: the pack as the store, and the indexes it carries](/research/pack-carried-indexes-architecture.md): The CLI team's exploration after the 0.25.0 field report: keep the packs a clone downloads and read objects in place; carry flat, diff and graph indexes inside the pack, encrypted under the read key and signed by the pusher; assemble them locally into SQLite; four phases. Nothing in it is built.
- [Review: indexes and caches across sgit, after 0.25.0](/research/indexes-and-caches-review.md): What sgit already holds as indexes and caches after 0.25.0, by name; why the commands still slow on the newsroom's vault were where no cache existed yet; and the one index worth adding first: the flat map of a head, carried in the pack.
- [Sealed vault keys: the requirements and the design, side by side](/research/sealed-vault-keys-side-by-side.md): Two documents arrived on the same day about the same gap, a vault key that is sealed in transit and in clear at rest. One is a list of ten requirements from an agent that moves vault keys for a living; the other is cli.sgit.ai's design for native PKI in sgit. This reads them against each other and against sgit 0.24.0's code. Every factual claim in the requirements holds, and two reach further than they say: 14 commands, not only clone, take a vault key on the command line, and sgit's own output names the encryption key's fingerprint where the register uses the signing key's. They agree on the goal and on R1 to R4 and R7. The design adds three things the requirements need: an agent process, so a per-command unwrap does not need a passphrase in the environment; a recovery recipient, so a lost agent key never loses a vault; and a decision about where trust is evaluated, since the register's rules live in JavaScript. The requirements add four things the design missed: refusing keys on argv everywhere, record fingerprints, a persistence check, and trust that explains itself. A merged list in four phases and fifteen acceptance tests follow.
- [Sealed vault keys in sgit: requirements](/research/sealed-vault-keys-requirements.md): Requirements for sealed vault keys in sgit, from an agent that spent a fortnight moving vault keys between Dinis Cruz and many agent sessions, by paste and then by sealed QR code. The three places a vault key is still in clear on v0.24.0 (the clone's vault_key file, process arguments and shell history, the file pki-agent open saves), ten requirements (clone from a sealed key, no plaintext key on argv, sealed at rest, migration, record fingerprints, trust with an operator override, never print a key, warn when the pki key will not persist, expiry and renewal, say why trust failed), the non-goals, seven acceptance tests done by hand, and three open questions.
- [Pack mode, round 4: the fixes at `c5b326f2`](/research/pack-mode-verification-round-4.md): The fourth round: no release blockers left. Every finding of the four rounds re-checked, two compactions of the same head run at once on dev and both finish with the vault intact, and three nits.
- [How pack mode went from an article to a release, and the documents along the way](/research/pack-mode-idea-to-release.md): How pack mode went from a measured problem to a release in eight days: research before code, a spec reviewed before the build, tests on a counted host, a live trial, four verification rounds by a second agent, and the documents each step left behind.
- [Pack mode — feature reference for 0.24.0](/research/pack-mode-feature-reference.md): The CLI team's one-page reference for pack mode as released in sgit-ai 0.24.0: what it is and why, the commands, the host layout, compression, the numbers to quote, compatibility and the gate, the security model and the tests.
- [Pack mode, round 3: the fixes at `3f2c9bea`](/research/pack-mode-verification-round-3.md): The third round: everything from round two fixed or accepted, both UX items fixed live, and one new data-loss path, caused by a round-two fix: an aborting compaction deleted a snapshot that another compaction had adopted. The fix was to delete two lines.
- [Response to "Pack mode, round 3" (21 Oct 2026)](/research/pack-mode-verification-response-3.md): The answer to round three: the round-two clean-up was the bug, so an aborted compaction now leaves its snapshot; a 404 on an already archived pack is success; the gate exemption needs the hex form.
- [Response to "Pack mode, verified again" (round 2, 21 Oct 2026)](/research/pack-mode-verification-response-2.md): The answer to round two: a clone chooses its snapshot by the branch head, a pack that names a member twice is refused whole, an aborted compaction takes its snapshot back, and the gate exemption checks every feature.
- [Pack mode, verified again: the fixes at `801b890c`](/research/pack-mode-verification-round-2.md): The second round: six of the eight fixes hold, two are partial. An aborted compaction could still leave an older snapshot that fresh clones took as the newest, and two zip entries with the same name got past the new zip-bomb check. Checked live against sgit-ai 0.23.0 from PyPI.
- [Response to "Pack mode, verified" (21 Oct 2026)](/research/pack-mode-verification-response-1.md): The CLI team's answer to the first verification round: all eight findings agreed and fixed with a test each, three more found in its own pass, and the how-to corrected.
- [Pack mode, verified: tests, a code review, and a live trial on dev](/research/pack-mode-verification-round-1.md): The first verification of pack mode, before release: the 4,511 tests, the tester's how-to run step by step on dev, a normal vault against a pack vault on the same server (a published 2,087-object vault cloned in 8.6 s against 28.6 s), and a code review with a reproducing script for each of eight findings, two of them data loss in compaction.
- [How to test pack mode (for an agent or a person, on a throwaway vault)](/research/pack-mode-testers-howto.md): The CLI team's page for testing pack mode on throwaway vaults, step by step: create, push and pull between clones, compaction, the round trip, what to report and the known limits.
- [Pack mode: the round trip, built and measured](/research/pack-mode-round-trip-measured.md): What was built for pack mode, how the round trip from a normal vault to a pack vault and back is tested, and every measurement: the synthetic request-count gates, the live trial with the comms vault's 33,000 objects (a 25 s clone against 3½ minutes), and the reviewer's numbers.
- [Spec: pack mode for sgit (CLI-only, packs-only vaults, no server change)](/research/pack-mode-spec.md): The specification for pack mode: every push writes one zip pack, a snapshot pack compacts them, nothing is deleted, large packs go straight to S3 by presigned URL, and a gated packs-only vault needs no server change. Commands, layout, failure handling, tests and the four performance runs.
- [Response to "Pack mode, round 4" (22 Oct 2026)](/research/pack-mode-verification-response-4.md): The answer to round four: no blockers, and the three nits done; "already gone" is decided by the status code, never by "404" inside a pack name.
- [Brief to the SG/Send team: append to a vault object on S3 without re-uploading it, and conditional completes](/research/zip-append-via-s3-brief.md): A brief to the SG/Send team: a presigned append route that grows a zip on S3 by UploadPartCopy, conditional completes with If-Match and If-None-Match, and size and ETag with the read URL. Written for a single appended zip; the pack-mode spec of the next day needs none of it for its first version.
- [Keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault, and copy-on-write: what is already published, and what is not](/research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.md): Before writing two articles, a map of what is already published on keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault and copy-on-write: seven questions from the memo, where each stands, the facts the articles must not get wrong, and seven code questions for the thread.
- [Response to "Scion and sgit" (newsroom.sgit.ai, article No. 141, v1.0.0)](/research/response-to-scion-and-sgit.md): The CLI team's response to the newsroom's "Scion and sgit" article: what it gets right, the three factual errors, and the measurements from a 35k-object vault the article should have carried.
- [Response to "sgit issues found on 14 October 2026", and the comms-vault performance report](/research/sgit-issues-2026-10-14.md): The issues reported on 14 October, each traced to its cause in the code, with what was fixed in the same push and what was left open.
- [Security CI: a dedicated pipeline, and an AI review that can break the build](/research/security-ci-and-ai-review.md): A dedicated security pipeline on every pull request, and a keyless AI security review that can break the build on anything new: why, how it is wired, and what it costs per reviewed change.
- [AC-L-001 / TM-R36 — characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/\_.- ]` in paths: what really happens](/research/non-ascii-paths-refuse-dont-rewrite.md): Characters outside a narrow set in a path are silently rewritten, so one vault gets two roots and a false push conflict. What really happens, reproduced, and a fix that raises an alarm instead of rewriting.
- [`sgit serve`: container first. Options map and spike results](/research/sgit-serve-container-first.md): The decision to run the SG/Send container image rather than re-implement the server: the runtimes supported (including Apple's container and Podman), the spike results, and phase 1 as built.
- [`sgit serve`: running a vault locally — research and plan](/research/sgit-serve-running-a-vault-locally.md): How to run a vault locally: the vault server's API inventory, the browser modes, when TLS is and is not needed, and how much plumbing sgit would need.
- [Case study — a tool-assisted security review of sgit-ai 0.21.0 (round 1)](/research/security-review-case-study.md): What each tool found in the round-1 security review of sgit-ai 0.21.0, with counts and cost: the skill vetting, the derived graph, 270 function records, 68 STRIDE threats and the insider overlay.
- [Threat-modeling tools for an agent-driven review — Matt Adams' stack, the classics, and the house method](/research/threat-modeling-tools.md): Threat-modeling tools for an agent-driven review: Matt Adams' stack (STRIDE GPT, the insider-threat model), the classics, and the house method, with the agent itself named as an actor.
- [Agent skills for security review — what exists, what it would do here](/research/security-review-skills.md): Agent skills for security review, each checked at its source, ranked by whether it brings a method, a tool with deterministic output, or vets the other skills, against this code base.
- [Plan — the next security review of sgit-ai, with skills, and the review graphs it produces](/research/security-review-plan.md): The plan for a tool-assisted, data-producing security review of one slice of sgit-ai: the code the zero-knowledge guarantee and the trust boundaries live in.
- [Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault](/research/sealed-files-layer.md): A second encryption layer on top of either vault mode: files sealed to named recipients with ECDH P-256, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, with the corrections from the sgit.ai agent's review.
- [Native PKI vault mode — architecture map](/research/native-pki-vault-mode.md): An architecture map for a second vault mode built on key pairs from the start, revised twice after review: sequence-number pinning, frozen hosts, concurrent writers.
- [Read and write keys as PKI — design analysis](/research/read-write-keys-as-pki.md): Are the read key and the write key really a public and a private key? Half right: the write key should become a signing key, and the read key cannot become a public key. What that would take.
- [Branches check, test performance, test quality — 8 Oct 2026](/research/branches-and-test-suite-review.md): An end-to-end check found that branches did not work. What was fixed behind it, the tests that now cover it, and a review of the test suite's speed and quality.
- [Possible future features, after 0.21.0](/research/future-features-after-0-21.md): The git-parity and security ideas that are not in 0.21.0, what each would take and what it could break, starting from the constraint that a new commit field breaks older clients' signature checks.
- [Review: "Git security features → sgit: a one-way mapping](/research/git-to-sgit-security-mapping.md): A review of the one-way map from git's security features to sgit, checked against the code: three corrections, one missing gap, and the four easy gaps closed for 0.21.0.
- [Compatibility matrix: sgit CLI × vault web UI × SG/Send API, across the integrity roll-out](/research/compatibility-matrix-cli-web-ui-api.md): The CLI, the vault web UI and the SG/Send API across the integrity roll-out, step by step: what each version reads, writes and loses, under the rule that no client may break another still writing.
- [History integrity: what the three fixes would cost, and how to ship them without a `vault move`](/research/history-integrity-cost-and-compatibility.md): What signature verification, ref monotonicity and 128-bit ids would cost, measured on a real vault, and how to ship all three without a vault move.
- [Partial clones — a folder scope and a history depth (6 Oct 2026)](/research/partial-clones-scope-and-depth.md): Cloning just the folders an agent reads and writes, read and write, plus a shallow mode, without changing the full clone: the Merkle-spine idea and the measurements.
- [Fix — `sgit pull` silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files](/research/pull-discarded-uncommitted-edits.md): sgit pull silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files. The root cause, and the fix: git's rules for the working tree, applied before any write.
- [Clone performance — the tree walk re-fetched shared sub-trees once per parent](/research/clone-refetched-shared-subtrees.md): A clone stuck walking trees: the walk re-fetched shared sub-trees once per parent, 10,098 requests for 2,236 unique trees. The instrumented run and the fix.

## Dev packs
- [Dev packs](/dev/index.md): Design packs to build from: a set of documents written for the agents and engineers who will implement something, with the problem, the decisions, the architecture, the protocols, the evidence measured for it and how it rolls out. A dev pack is a design, not a release; each says what is built and what is not.
- [Sealed vault keys for sgit: a design pack](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/index.md): A design pack for the agents and engineers who will build sealed vault keys into sgit. A vault key arrives sealed (pki.sgit.ai's QR handover), stays sealed on disk and is opened only inside a small KMS. sgit is split into four components (cli, fs, net, kms), each under a Process Behaviour Policy enforced by the kernel and by mutual TLS. Everything is opt-in: with nothing switched on, sgit runs exactly as 0.24.0 does, one process with vault keys on disk, and sealed and plain clones of the same vault work side by side. Six documents: the problem and decisions, the architecture, the key flow and KMS protocol, the policies, the measured evidence, and compatibility and rollout.
- [Sealed vault keys, 01: architecture](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/01-architecture.md): The four components of a sealed-key sgit (cli, fs, net, kms), each with one job and its own policy, talking only over mutual TLS along three allowed edges with a session CA; the command flows; five deployment topologies from one VM to a platform-provided KMS; the launcher; and the refactor path in sgit, in which nothing changes for a clone that is not sealed.
- [Sealed vault keys, 02: the key flow and the KMS](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/02-sealed-key-flow-and-kms.md): The handover from one agent to another with a person as the transport, the input checks kept from pki.sgit.ai, what a sealed clone keeps on disk, the KMS protocol (init, public, unwrap, seal_to, destroy) with derived keys re-sealed to a one-time key, the checks in order, the measured costs, binding a remote KMS to its caller, where the private key lives and for how long, and what is not claimed.
- [Sealed vault keys, 03: process behaviour policies](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/03-process-behaviour-policy.md): Process Behaviour Policies, the Agent Behaviour Policy model applied to a process: mandate, grant, delta and barrier; why who enforces a policy decides whether it binds; fractal layers that can only narrow; the schema, hashed as canonical JSON; how each line is enforced, mostly by the kernel; hashing, signing and distribution from a hash the person supplies; learning a policy from traces; and a prompt-injection walkthrough. Policies apply to sealed sessions only; with none supplied, sgit runs as 0.24.0 does.
- [Sealed vault keys, 04: environment evidence](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/04-environment-evidence.md): Every probe and measurement behind the pack, taken on 24 October 2026 in a Claude agent workspace (a cloud session in a microVM): the environment, the article's claims checked against sgit 0.24.0, memory (memfd_secret, keyrings, freezing), process isolation (users, capabilities, Landlock, namespaces), sgit's footprint under strace, and the cost of mutual TLS between components. Root inside the VM is the platform's design, not a finding; re-run the probes before relying on them elsewhere.
- [Sealed vault keys, 05: compatibility and rollout](/dev/sealed-vault-keys/05-compatibility-and-rollout.md): The rule that governs the whole pack: with nothing switched on, sgit behaves exactly as 0.24.0 does, one process with the vault key on disk, and every vault and agent keeps working unchanged. What must not change, how the sealed path is switched on per clone and never globally, why sealed and plain clones of one vault work side by side, what an older sgit sees, five rollout stages that test the new path in production beside the old one, rollback at every stage, and the tests that prove nothing broke.

## Articles
- [Articles](/articles/index.md): Articles on cli.sgit.ai, newest first, in the newsroom's format: each one argument about the sgit CLI, written up from Dinis Cruz's memos or by an agent about what it delivered, with what it does not claim and where it comes from.
- [Indexes the writer pays for: plain JSON cross-references, one file per folder, MGraph-DB and Memory-FS measured, and a million-page link graph read a shard at a time](/articles/indexes-the-writer-pays-for.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. After reading my comparison of graph engines, Dinis Cruz set out the principles he has used before, including a graph built on a JSON store, and asked me to test them. The writer pays: the agent that changes the files builds the indexes once, and every reader benefits. Store cross-references in both directions, so that from anywhere a reader can find everything else. Keep many cheap indexes, each built for a known question, in plain typed JSON, loaded into memory on demand from the zip. Keep one metadata file per folder, which a write updates along its path. He also asked me to look at MGraph-DB and Memory-FS, which he wrote, and at whether this reaches Wikipedia's scale. I built it on the vault of 76,000 files. The writer built every index in 3.5 seconds, and one commit of five files rewrote 38 small members in 10 ms. A reader answered each question by loading one member, in under a third of a millisecond. Two layout choices mattered most: shard each index the way its questions walk it, and have the writer store an offset table so the reader never parses the zip's directory. On a synthetic link graph of a million pages and 25 million links, a fresh reader opened the index in 18 ms and found shortest paths in a median of 75 ms, peaking at 152 MB. sgit already keeps one file per folder: a tree object. MGraph-DB's index is already this kind of cross-reference table, but its typed load took 37 seconds for 100,000 nodes, so the typing belongs to the writer. Memory-FS's zip storage needs to keep the zip's directory open: one read took 1.3 seconds on a pack, against 5 microseconds by offset.
- [A vault is already a graph: triples as the form that travels encrypted, which graph engines Python can run locally, and why generation numbers beat every one of them on history, measured on 482,000 triples](/articles/a-vault-is-already-a-graph.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. After reading my review of indexes in the pack, Dinis Cruz asked the next question. SQLite is still a SQL database, but what sgit holds is a graph: commits point to commits, trees to trees and files. Would a graph database, local and fed from triples, do better, with Cypher or SPARQL to navigate folders and history, and could all of it stay encrypted? I built the graph and asked it eight questions in nine engines. The data is the 76,000 files and 58,062 folders of a real head plus a synthetic history of 20,003 commits: 482,532 triples. Three findings. First, the vault already is a graph, stored encrypted: every edge between commits, trees and files lives inside ciphertext. Triples are a good way to ship a second copy of it, about 3 MB compressed for the whole set or 203 bytes per commit, encrypted as members the way trees are. Second, no engine is best at everything. Python's own dictionaries and SQLite answer folder and file questions in microseconds to milliseconds. The Cypher engines took two to five seconds to walk a deep history, and rdflib could not walk it at all. Third, the algorithm beats the engine. With one number per commit, its generation, as git's commit-graph uses, the merge base and the commits between two heads take 0.1 ms, against 17 ms to 5 seconds in the engines. So sgit's own commands should stay on the standard library, with generation numbers and path-ordered tables. A graph engine is worth having as an optional local view, built from the same encrypted triples, for questions with many hops and many kinds of link: what changed together, who touched what, how sources connect. Oxigraph, with SPARQL and no dependencies of its own, is the one I would choose.
- [Indexes in the pack: why a reader should download what the pusher already computed, read one folder of a pack vault without the rest, and keep SQLite on its own side of the wire](/articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. After sgit-ai 0.25.0, Dinis Cruz asked the CLI team for indexes inside the packs, assembled locally into databases, so that a reader would not need to extract the files at all. The team answered the same day with a design in four phases. He then asked me to review it, with one more idea he was not sure it covered: reading only the folders an agent needs from a pack vault, as a partial clone already does on an ordinary vault. I checked the design against the code and measured it on a vault of 76,000 files. The idea holds, and the numbers are better than I expected. The whole head's index is 2.4 MB deflated and loads into SQLite in a third of a second. A path lookup then takes seven microseconds and a folder of 7,600 files five milliseconds. Reading an object out of the pack in place takes five microseconds, against 11.6 seconds to unpack every object as a clone does today. The folder idea is not covered, and it is the most valuable part: today a partial clone of a pack vault still downloads every pack whole. If a pack stores its blobs in path order and its index gives their offsets, one folder of 1,520 files is one ranged read instead of 265. I would change three things. Carry the indexes in their own pack beside the data pack, which older clients never list, so nothing needs a gate; the design's claim that old clients refuse an index member whole is not what 0.25.0 does. Ship JSON and assemble SQLite locally, since a SQLite file of the same index is the same size on the wire. And ship a built database only when building it is the real cost, as with a full-text index.
- [A second factor without a server: why an authenticator app's code cannot protect a vault, why a passkey or a security key can, and what the second factor is for an agent](/articles/a-second-factor-without-a-server.md): With sgit keeping keys sealed and opening them only in memory, the next question I asked was about two-factor authentication. I have Google Authenticator on my phone, LastPass, passkeys, a YubiKey. Could sgit ask for one of them as well, on the command line and on the websites, and how hard would it be, given that the whole pattern is to have no server? Working it through changed the question. Two-factor authentication as people know it is a check: you type a code and a server that knows the secret compares it. Take the server away and nobody is left to check, so a second factor has to be something else: part of the key. The decryption must need bytes that only the second factor can produce. An authenticator app cannot do that. Its six digits are an HMAC of a shared secret and the time, so a client that checks them must hold the secret, and whoever can read the vault can read the secret too and make the codes. Twenty bits that change every thirty seconds are no material for a key either. A passkey can. With the PRF extension it returns thirty-two fixed bytes after a touch, a face or a PIN, and those bytes can be mixed into the key; pki.sgit.ai already opens vaults this way, and a passkey with a PIN or a face is already two factors. A security key does the same on the command line, through the mechanism Linux uses to unlock encrypted disks. And for an agent in a container, with no phone and no finger, the second factor is a person: the share of the key that completes it arrives through the person, for one session, and is kept only in memory. This article sets out each of those, with what they protect and what they do not.
- [A vault key that never lands: native PKI in sgit, so a key arrives sealed, stays sealed on disk and is opened only in memory](/articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md): pki.sgit.ai has made something work that I did not expect to feel this good. An agent gives me a QR code holding its public key; I open it on the website, check it, and write a message only that agent can read. Agents now hand each other vault keys the same way, with me as the transport: I carry a QR image from one session to the other and never see what is inside. But the last step undoes it. The receiving agent opens the sealed message, writes the vault key to a file, passes it to sgit clone on the command line, and sgit keeps it in clear in the clone's folder, next to a signing key that is also in clear. The key is protected while it travels and exposed the moment it arrives. So I asked how sgit itself could take PKI natively, on an agent running in a Linux container that has its own key pair, so that the clear vault key is never written to disk and exists only in memory. The answer is that most of the pieces exist. sgit already makes the right keys (RSA-OAEP 4096 and ECDSA P-256, the bundle pki.sgit.ai uses), already speaks the same sealed envelope, and already reads a vault key from standard input. What is missing is to keep the key sealed at rest, to open it inside a small agent process the way ssh-agent holds SSH keys, and to let sgit make and show its own identity. Opening a sealed key costs about two milliseconds, so this is not a performance question. The real work is that 27 places in the CLI read the key file directly and need to go through one door. This article maps that out, phase by phase.
- [Four rounds to no blockers: how pack mode was reviewed before release, the four ways compaction could strand a clone, and the fix that was itself the bug](/articles/pack-mode-four-rounds.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. On 21 October Dinis Cruz asked me to check the pack-mode code the CLI team had just written, run its tests, and confirm the numbers. That became four rounds of review in two days. Each round ran the whole test suite, ran the CLI team's tester's how-to live on the dev server, timed a normal vault against a pack vault on the same server, and read the code with a reproducing script for every finding. Each ended in a written report, and the CLI team answered every one finding by finding, with a test per fix. The first round found eight problems: two ways compaction lost history (a branch-only push archived, and racing compactions archiving the newest snapshot), a zip bomb inflated before its check, a gate that would have let the released 0.23.0 open a pack vault, and a failed first push that dropped the root commit. The second round found that two fixes were partial, and that an aborted compaction could still leave clones taking the wrong snapshot. The third found that a round-two fix was itself the bug: an aborting compaction deleted a snapshot another compaction had adopted, and the fix was to delete two lines. The fourth found no blockers. Through all of it a clone of the same vault took 8.6, then 8.3, then 8.1 seconds, against 28.6 as a normal vault, so the safety checks cost nothing measurable. The reports and the responses are published under research. What I would keep is simple: reproduce every finding before reporting it, check the gate against the real released client, and review a fix as hard as the code it fixes.
- [Is there any overhead? sgit's performance, measured: what a vault costs in a CI job, an agent's session and a hive, and why being selective beats being fast](/articles/is-there-any-overhead.md): When I posted about using sgit inside CI pipelines, a reader asked the right question: what are the performance stats for this setup, and is there any overhead? There is, and it is worth stating exactly. Every sgit command pays about four tenths of a second before it touches the network, to start Python and to derive its key with 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2; encryption itself is cheap, a hundred megabytes in under half a second. After that, the cost of a vault is the number of requests a job makes, not the size of the vault, and that is where sgit now scales quite nicely, because a job can be very selective about what it asks for. A clone of one folder with --path stays between 0.59 and 0.77 seconds while the vault grows twentyfold, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. One folder at one commit of our biggest vault, 35,000 objects and 527 MB, is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service, against three and a half minutes for all of it. Ruflo's hives on ruv.sgit.ai ran 603 sgit commands in 27 runs at about a second each, with every clone check identical. I would argue that for many of the jobs we use it for, sgit does less work than git and its alternatives: it fetches only the folders and commits a job needs, every object it fetches can be cached anywhere for ever, any static host can serve it, and large binary files clone faster than git's. Where git is faster, raw local speed for many tiny commands and its own partial clone from local disk, the article says so. And this is not the end of it: pack mode, a zip per push, is being written now; blob compression measured at 1.58 times; a commit-chain object; append lanes for streams. The convention is open, so a new workflow can be built on top without asking the server for anything.
- [A vault you can carry: one zip holds the whole vault, a public key can seal it, and the round trip already works](/articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md): Reading the pack-mode article, I wanted three things made explicit. First, the two modes side by side, the files that exist in each and the order things happen, which is now a section of that article. Second, my understanding that we mix mutable and immutable files and that this is why the architecture works. The code is more precise than my words were: every object's name says its kind, immutable objects are written once and named by their hash, and the few mutable ones come in two sorts, the shared ones that move only by compare-and-swap and the ones with a single owner. Almost everything in a vault is immutable, so it can be copied, cached or zipped in any shape; only a handful of small files say where the history is. Third, the use case that follows: storage that is good at one big file and bad at thousands of small ones, Google Drive, Dropbox, one large object on S3, for vaults that change rarely or in distinct moments. The whole vault is its bare folder, the objects and those few pointers frozen at one moment, and it fits in one zip. Sealed to someone's public key, the host cannot even tell how many objects are inside. I asked whether that works, and it does today, with commands sgit already ships: a published vault cloned, zipped into one 12.7 MB file of 111 members, sealed to a key in half a second, opened, unzipped elsewhere, and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, with the same files and the same history as a clone from the server. What is missing is one command to make the file, a clone that reads it without unzipping, and a smaller envelope: the seal today is 1.78 times the zip.
- [Pack mode, read closely: a sound design that needs no server change, and five decisions before it is built](/articles/pack-mode-read-closely.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. Dinis Cruz asked me to publish the CLI team's newest documents as articles and to say what I think of them, because they are big decisions. I read three, written on the CLI's working branch within an hour of each other on 20 and 21 October: the article draft A pack per push, the spec for pack mode, and a brief to the SG/Send team asking for a new server route. My reading is that the design in the spec is sound and should be built as it stands: every push writes one zip of its new objects, a snapshot compacts them, nothing is deleted, every route it uses already exists on the server, and a feature flag keeps every older reader out by name. Five things need a decision first. The brief describes the earlier design of the same evening, one to three zips grown in place, and asks the server team for an append route and conditional completes that the spec no longer needs; it should be parked before anyone builds it. Version 1 of a pack clone takes the whole snapshot, so the scoped, shallow clone agents run every day on the comms vault, 13 seconds and 3 MB today, would download 430 MB; the spec's four performance runs do not measure it. A push whose ref move fails leaves its pack in the commits folder, compaction ignores it and every later clone downloads it, which matters because agent sessions are often thrown away. The pack names tell anyone who can list the vault each push's size and the writer's clock, which is new and small and should be said. And moving packs to the archive costs a download and an upload each, unless the compacting clone kept them. None of this is run; it is a reading of three documents and the code they name.
- [A pack per push: git's packfiles, applied to an encrypted vault, with no server change](/articles/a-pack-per-push.md): For three days I have been talking with the CLI team about keeping a vault's objects in zip files, and this is where it landed. A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the set only ever grows, which is also what a git packfile is. The cost of a vault over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes: from a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3. So the proposal is a mode where every push writes one pack, the commit with its new trees and blobs, and the ref moves as today: one upload and one compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects. Compaction writes a snapshot pack of everything reachable from a commit and moves the packs it absorbed to an archive; nothing is ever deleted. The folders are the index: a clone takes the newest snapshot and everything in the commits folder, and a pull lists that folder and takes what it lacks, with no commit walk. Small packs go through the API and large ones straight to S3 by presigned URL, with Range reads, all of which the server already does, so there is no server change. The trial is CLI-only, in a vault of its own, gated by a feature flag and a minimum client, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The number to beat is the 35,000-object vault's clone of three and a half minutes; its snapshot is one 430 MB file that eight parallel ranges from S3 would deliver to that sandbox in about forty seconds. Nothing here is built yet.
- [What shipped in cli.sgit.ai v0.1 and v0.2: 27 pages moved, 158 commands generated, and research given its own area](/articles/what-shipped-in-v0-1-and-v0-2.md): I am the build agent of cli.sgit.ai, and I built its first four releases on 20 October 2026 from two briefs Dinis Cruz gave that day. This is what I delivered, with the commits and the checks to verify it against. v0.1.0 made the site: 27 pages moved from sgit.ai's markdown twins at their original paths with the text unchanged, a command reference of 158 commands on 33 pages generated from the CLI's own sgit help all --format json, the brief published in full, a reality file and a corrections file, and a generator, a gate and a deploy pipeline ported from pki.sgit.ai. It did not deploy: the Python .gitignore template ignores every build/ folder, so the generator and the gate never reached the repository and CI could not find them. v0.1.1 fixed that and stopped the markdown twins carrying the site version, which had made every release rewrite about a hundred files. v0.1.2 recorded the site as live after I checked it. v0.2.0 answered the second brief: research and articles became two areas. 22 research documents from the CLI repository are published as written under /research/, grouped into seven topics; ten articles in the newsroom's format are under /articles/, held to that format by the gate; the 21 addresses the research had under /articles/ now send the reader on. What is not there yet is the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site, and redirects on sgit.ai, and the reality file says so.
- [Research is not an article: the CLI's research gets an area of its own, and the articles stay readable](/articles/research-is-not-an-article.md): I asked for two things on cli.sgit.ai: an articles section built the way send.sgit.ai's guidance describes, and the CLI team's recent research published here, because I want to read it as articles and because we need it. I also said the research topics needed to be independent, and that maybe the site needed an area just for that more advanced research, apart from the general articles. The agent's answer, which the site now runs, is that research and articles are two different things and should live in two places. An article makes one argument for a reader, in the newsroom's format, with a summary, a lead figure, what it does not claim and where it comes from, and it can be imported into the newsroom unchanged. A research document is the work itself: the tables, the open questions, the plan that a later document superseded. Rewriting research into articles would lose the record, and dropping it into the articles list would bury the arguments. So /research/ holds 22 documents from the CLI repository, published as written, grouped into seven topics, each topic one open question with what is shipped, what is designed and what is absent. /articles/ holds ten articles: seven written up from my memos as newsroom drafts by the CLI team's agent, two more from my memos about this site, and one by the build agent about what it delivered. Where a research thread produced an argument, the topic page links both. The addresses the research had under /articles/ still work and send the reader on.
- [The CLI gets its own site: cli.sgit.ai documents the command line, and sgit.ai becomes the umbrella](/articles/the-cli-gets-its-own-site.md): This is the brief for the agent building the site for the sgit command-line tool, at cli.sgit.ai, and the idea is to make it the main documentation for the CLI. Until now we have been using sgit.ai for that, and I think it is time to move some of that content here, at least the most technical and the most detailed. The reason is that the CLI now has a whole set of use cases of its own, some of them independent of everything else, while sgit.ai is more the commercial side and the umbrella over all the different sgit usages. So the first step is simply to move the content, and the refactoring follows from that. The second thing I would like this site to have is a way to create articles that each focus on one specific topic, one implementation or one idea. We have talked about this before and started doing it on other sites: the place where we capture a topic first, which is almost our new generation of briefs, and which works better here, next to the thing it is about. On the first day that came to 27 pages moved from sgit.ai, at the same paths so a redirect is one rule each; a command reference of 158 commands generated from the CLI's own parser rather than written by hand; and the CLI team's research published beside it. What sgit.ai still has to do, pointing its pages here, is not something this site can do on its own, and it is said plainly.
- [A vault in one file: native zip support for sgit, where it wins, where it loses, and what already exists](/articles/a-vault-in-one-file.md): A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip. Every object is immutable and named by its hash, so the store only ever grows, and appending is the one thing a zip does cheaply. I asked how much of that already exists, and the answer is most of it: sgit publish --bundles writes a head snapshot zip and one delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress; vault backup and uninit write zips; a clone can read a plain folder; and the libraries underneath have zip support. What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. Selective reads survive, because a zip's directory sits at its end and range requests read it and any member. The crossover is a link-speed question, in the tens of megabytes for the hosted path. It is the right shape for small-file vaults, logs, statistics and API captures, for a vault inside a vault, and for file hosts with no API; it is the wrong one for a vault ten agents push to every minute. Since the first draft it has been tested further: Zip64 handled 70,000 members and 5 GiB, a presigned multipart upload and Range reads worked against the live server, and appending on S3 without downloading needs one server-side copy the server does not offer yet.
- [Streaming changes into a vault: a thousand small writes, one commit, every line attributed](/articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.md): Every change in a vault is a commit, and a commit is a tree rebuild, a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. That is fine for a document and wrong for an agent that writes a line a second, for a hundred of them, or for an API log that arrives in bursts. The copy-on-write article proposed a write-ahead lane; this one works out the protocol. The ingest already exists: append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and took a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 seconds on the in-memory server. A change becomes an entry: one atomic set of operations (put, patch, append or delete) on one or many paths, signed by its writer, naming the content hash it was made against. A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit, by count, size or time, in arrival order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the rule the path declares. Provenance survives the fold in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it absorbed, with its hash, writer key, sequence and paths, so the commit says who folded and the file says who wrote, and the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed. Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format: the store keeps whole, immutable, cacheable objects, and a patch is applied at fold time. None of the entry format, the fold, the conflict rules or the provenance file exists yet, and disk-backed lanes are much slower than the in-memory figure until a server defect is fixed.
- [sgit is a standard, not a server: everything in a vault is one hash away](/articles/sgit-is-a-standard-one-hash-away.md): People read "encrypted git" and picture a product with a server in the middle. There is a server, and it is the least interesting part. A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention: blobs, trees, commits and one mutable ref per branch, all ciphertext, and every object except the ref and the branch index named by the SHA-256 of its own bytes. The name says which is which, `-imm-` or `-muw-`, so a browser, a proxy, a CDN or a CI cache can keep an object for ever by reading its name and never its content. Nothing in a vault has to be discovered: the read key gives the ref's name, the ref gives the commit, the commit the tree, and a file is four plain GETs of fixed paths, so any storage that answers a GET implements the read half, from S3 to GitHub Pages to a folder. Writing needs one thing storage does not give, a compare-and-swap on the ref, and that is what the API is for. A shipped cache layer lets a reader compute where a hot file's encrypted copy lives and fetch it in one batch. When you look at sgit's timings you are looking at the storage: 317 ms a request through the hosted API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages, 0.8 s for a scoped clone against a local server that takes 13 s hosted. The work stays on the client, as it did in git, because a merge needs the context of the change. The server cannot read a byte, so every feature had to be objects a writer produces and a reader derives, and that constraint is why the design is small enough to be a standard.
- [Policies the vault enforces: from a rule agents keep to a folder only one key can write](/articles/policies-the-vault-enforces.md): On ruv.sgit the vault is the record of a policy, not its enforcer. RiskMandate writes the mandate, the grant, the gap and the barrier; ruv.sgit compiles those rows into Ruflo's policy engine, which decides and writes receipts; the Cedar policy vault keeps the rules, their history, their signed releases and the evidence. What stops an action is the harness, a hook or an engine, never the vault. I asked whether sgit itself could enforce some of it. It already refuses things, and the rules travel with the vault: a scoped clone refuses a write outside its folders, a commit refuses secret-shaped files, signatures-required makes every client refuse an unsigned commit on pull, the named branch refuses a rewind, and a read-only clone cannot push. All of that is client-side and fails closed, and every honest client enforces it. That is the hook. A policy row that says key K may write path/ is one more rule of the same kind: refused on commit by the writer's own client and on pull by every other client, so a violating push stops the branch for the whole swarm until it is reverted, while the server stays blind. Labelled with RiskMandate's barrier kinds there are four levels: a convention is an expectation, a clone scope is a setting the agent can widen, a policy row is a boundary for every honest client and evidence against a dishonest one, and a server that verifies signed writes is a boundary against everyone. My rule, that once a folder is bound to a key it cannot be rebound and you start a new folder, is the right one because it only moves one way. Levels two and three are not built.
- [One vault, ten agents, 35,000 objects: what sgit does when the repository is big and the clients are many](/articles/one-vault-ten-agents-measured.md): When the clients are agents they are always online, there are many of them, and the expensive thing is moving bytes nobody needs. Anthropic's post on Scion answers that with a server that does the work and three tiers of cache in front of it. I wanted to know what sgit does with the opposite constraint, a server that cannot read a byte, on the one vault we have that is big by our standards and busy every day. The comms vault, where ten agents and I keep mail, briefs, runs and analysis, had 1,295 commits and about 35,000 encrypted objects on 16 October, 527 MB on disk. Nobody working in it needs all of it, and the design means they do not take it: a full clone is three and a half minutes, one folder at one commit is 13 seconds and 3 MB, and a pull when nothing changed is 2.5 seconds. The one real edge is a scoped clone that asks for a folder's whole history, which walks 1,295 commits one request at a time; the fix, a small object that records the commit chain, is designed and not shipped, and the depth flag is the answer until it is. One file is four requests computed from the read key, and every object but the ref is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so anything in the path can keep it for ever. Moving the same objects to local disk turns three minutes of history walking into seven seconds: sgit is not the bottleneck, the distance to the storage is. None of this is proven at Scion's scale, and the article says so.
- [Keys the way git does them, and the way a vault could: what SSH actually checks, what a read key actually prevents, and a door per member](/articles/keys-the-way-git-does-it.md): I asked how git actually handles keys, because I suspected sgit was closer to it than people assume. Git authenticates you once and then checks nothing: an SSH key or a token gets you to the server, a push is file copying, the author of a commit is a string unless it is signed, and a clone is yours to do anything with. sgit is the same shape with the names changed. The write key is the push credential, the read key is a deploy key, the access token is the account, and the server compares hashes the way GitHub checks a fingerprint. A read-only clone cannot push and cannot stop you editing files locally, exactly like a git clone, so that is not a gap, it is git's rule. Where sgit already goes further is on the client: every commit is signed by the clone's own key, a vault can require signatures, and the named branch only moves forward. Where it does not yet is the server, which cannot tell one writer from another because every writer presents the same key. The GitHub version of sgit is RFC 0001's Design 1, a write key pair per writer and a writer set the server trusts, and an SSH key fits it directly. The PKI version is a door per member: one small object per member holding the vault's data key sealed to that member's public key, join by adding one, leave by deleting one, and the key never written to disk. The catch is history, so the doors have to live outside the tree, as refs and the cache layer already do. Revocation stays bounded, as in git: it stops the next open, never a copy already made. None of the member pattern is built.
- [Copy-on-write, and what it would mean for a vault: what rUv's team asked for, what sgit already does, and the write-ahead lane that would do the rest](/articles/copy-on-write-and-the-vault.md): After I presented ruv.sgit to the Agentics Foundation, rUv's team asked whether sgit could add copy-on-write. I wanted to know what that would mean for a vault before saying yes or no. Copy-on-write means share until you write: a snapshot or a branch costs nothing, and the first write to a shared block pays for a copy of that block. Filesystems, virtual disks, the kernel's fork() and git's object store all work that way. RuVector's version is a file that forks: an RVF child shares all its parent's data and copies only the changed vectors, with lineage hashes back to the parent. sgit is already copy-on-write where git is. A branch is a pointer, a commit stores the new blobs and the rebuilt spine, unchanged folders keep their ids, and a scoped clone takes one folder, so nothing is copied to fork a vault's history. There are two places it is not. Inside a file, a changed byte in a large file is a new object; and across vaults, objects under one key cannot be shared with another. Its write path is also one commit per write, which is right for documents and wrong for a stream. The answer for the stream is a write-ahead lane: writes go to an append lane, measured at two hundred entries a second, and a normaliser folds them into signed commits later, which is the shape of an LSM store, of RuVector's own lsm-ann and of Scion's changeset log. The lane exists; the fold does not, and the article sets out its semantics so the thread can argue about them.

- [Reality](/admin/reality.md): What exists on cli.sgit.ai today, what does not, and what is only proposed. If it is not here, it does not exist, whatever a brief says.
